strengths: Well-motivated problem and framework: The preliminary experiment (Figure 1) convincingly demonstrates that an existing unified MLLM (Janus-Pro-7B) frequently fails to discriminate fine-grained object-level differences, providing a clear justification for the object-centric design.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: three benchmarks (T2I-CompBench++, DPGBench, GenEval), three backbones (Janus-Pro-7B, UniTok-MLLM-7B, Janus-1.3B), and extensive ablations on loss terms, filtering/selection, and prompt densification (Tables 4-6) support the core claims.

Self-improving design that does not rely on external datasets or reward models at training time is practically valuable, and the paper demonstrates generalization across architectures and model scales (Table 3).

The data construction pipeline (perturbation-based hard negatives via Replace/Swap/Drop, Decompositional VQA filtering, model-uncertainty selection) is thoughtfully engineered and each component is ablated, showing gains are not incidental.

Thoughtful consideration of confirmation bias: Table 10 quantifies the agreement between the self-model and an external VQA (Qwen-VL-2.5-7B), and Table 11 shows training with an external VQA scorer yields comparable results, partially addressing a key failure mode of self-improving frameworks.

Good reproducibility: implementation details (Table 7), full prompt templates, and training settings are provided in the appendix, and qualitative examples (Figures 3, 9-14) illustrate the claimed failure modes and improvements.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental. The core ingredients—DPO/SimPO-style preference optimization, VQA-based data filtering, and prompt perturbation for hard negatives—are all borrowed from prior work; the main new element is applying them with an explicit object-level focus in unified MLLMs. The contribution is largely an integration and engineering effort rather than a fundamentally new method.

The claim of outperforming diffusion-based models (e.g., DALL-E 3) on T2I-CompBench++ is made without caveat. Autoregressive unified MLLMs are known to be favored by VQA/CLIP-based compositional metrics, and the paper reports no image-quality/fidelity or human evaluation to support the stronger interpretation. The qualitative examples in the appendix also show limited photorealism, so the advantage is metric-specific and should be framed more carefully.

Improvements over the strongest baselines are modest in several places. On GenEval OSPO (0.82) is not the best (T2I-R1 is 0.84), and on DPGBench the gain over T2I-R1 (85.34 vs 85.09) is small. The paper sometimes emphasizes aggregates that favor its method (e.g., T2I-CompBench++) without equal emphasis on these borderline cases.

Baseline coverage is uneven. Strong recent self-improving baselines such as UniRL and DSR are only evaluated on secondary backbones or not at all on the main Janus-Pro-7B backbone (Table 3), making a fully like-for-like comparison of the framework against competing self-improving approaches difficult.

The self-rewarding filtering relies on internal VQA scores, and Table 10 shows the self-model systematically assigns higher VQA scores than the external model; the paper argues this is harmless based on Table 11, but this is only shown for one backbone and one metric threshold. Robustness to the fixed threshold τ=0.5 for filtering is not analyzed.

Training-data scale is limited (19k prompts). Although Figure 6 suggests plateauing, the scaling behavior on DPGBench/GenEval and the effect of densification quality on output fidelity are not fully disentangled from overall data quantity/quality effects.
The main text lacks a related-work section (deferred to the appendix), which hinders the reader's ability to situate the contributions relative to prior self-improving T2I methods.
